subtitle: Trauma-informed leadership makes your interactions as a leader more predictable, respectful and responsive. It does this while still protecting privacy, keeping accountability and meeting the agency’s actual responsibilities.
scope: For DHS leaders and supervisors. This course applies general trauma-informed principles to practice leadership and work-process situations. It does not teach clinical assessment, trauma treatment, crisis intervention or investigation, and does not alter employment, accommodation, safety, reporting or service requirements.
introTranscript: Leaders do not need to know a colleague’s personal history to make a meeting clearer, explain a decision respectfully or offer a meaningful choice. A trauma-informed approach helps us examine how routine practices may create avoidable uncertainty or pressure and how to respond more thoughtfully. This course connects that perspective to ordinary DHS leadership: giving notice, listening without forced disclosure, handling a difficult conversation, supporting appropriate help and reviewing the process. It keeps accountability and formal duties in place. The cases are practice, and the course provides no diagnosis or treatment. Use the lessons at your own pace, and keep private employee and recipient information out of practice activities.

lessons.title: Use a trauma-informed lens without diagnosing people
lessons.summary: Apply the principles to the interaction and work process, not as a way to infer a person’s history or condition.
lessons.objective: Explain how a general trauma-informed principle can inform a practice leadership practice.
objectives: Explain how a general trauma-informed principle can inform a practice leadership practice.
Distinguish supportive leadership from trauma assessment or treatment.
Replace an assumed personal explanation with a concrete process question.
takeaways: Improve the interaction without requiring a personal history.
A principle is a lens for practice, not a diagnosis.
Keep actual safety, personnel and clinical responsibilities distinct.
lessons.statement: You can make the process more respectful without deciding what someone has experienced.

image.caption: The focus is the leader’s practice and its effect, not a label placed on a colleague.

intro.heading: Start with what leadership can change
intro.body:
A practice leader sees an employee withdraw during a meeting and concludes that the employee must have experienced trauma. The leader then asks for the story in front of the team. This response is intrusive and unsupported. The observation may prompt a respectful process question, but it does not establish a personal history or authorize a clinical assessment.

CDC’s summary of the SAMHSA framework identifies six principles: safety; trustworthiness and transparency; peer support; collaboration and mutuality; empowerment, voice and choice; and cultural, historical and gender issues. In this course, use those principles to examine ordinary leadership practices. Could the meeting purpose be clearer? Are choices real? Is a decision explained? Does the process assume everyone communicates in the same way? These are questions about the work, not conclusions about a colleague.

A trauma-informed lens does not mean that every uncomfortable conversation is harmful or that leaders stop addressing responsibilities. It asks how necessary conversations and decisions can be conducted more thoughtfully. A leader can explain a work expectation clearly, offer appropriate preparation, listen to relevant information and retain the actual standard. That is different from either avoiding accountability or using pressure to force a personal disclosure.

Distinguish supportive practice from specialized duties. Clinical assessment and treatment belong with qualified professionals. Accommodation, reporting, safety and personnel matters retain their authorized processes. An urgent actual safety concern follows its immediate route; it does not wait for a reflective learning activity. MMB’s Leadership and Team Dynamics page offers a current route for appropriate leadership support, but this course does not promise a clinical service or invent its terms.

Begin with one practice you control. A surprise agenda can become a clear purpose and relevant advance information. A public personal question can become a private task-focused inquiry. A vague decision can become an explanation of what is decided and what remains open. Review the practical effect without claiming that one technique makes the whole organization trauma-informed or guarantees how every employee will feel.

inThisLesson: Keep specialized duties in their proper routes.
lessons.keyStatement: Apply the lens to your leadership behavior, not as an explanation of another person’s life.

flashcards.back: A way of examining interactions and practices through principles such as safety, transparency and choice. It is not a clinical assessment.
Something seen or heard in the task. It can support a respectful question without proving a private history or motive.
Clear, respectful work practices and an appropriate route for help. It does not make a supervisor a clinician.
Ongoing attention across practices and processes. One workshop or checklist does not establish it by itself.

accordion.heading: Keep the lens within its proper scope

items.title: Describe the practice before the person
items.body: “The meeting had no clear agenda and asked for personal stories” identifies a design choice. “The employee must be traumatized” makes a claim about the person that the observation cannot establish. The process description points to something the leader can examine and change.

items.title: Retain meaningful accountability
items.body: A necessary work expectation can be stated with a clear purpose, relevant facts and a chance to respond. Respectful practice does not require abandoning an actual obligation. It asks the leader to remove unnecessary surprise, humiliation or coercion from the way the conversation occurs.

items.title: Avoid a certification claim
items.body: Completing this course shows participation in learning, not organizational certification or a clinical qualification. The CDC summary emphasizes continuing organizational attention. A practical improvement should be described for what it changes rather than as proof of a complete transformation.

tabs.label: Leader
tabs.body: In the practice meeting, the leader can provide a clear purpose, relevant information and a task-focused way to respond. Those choices concern the interaction and may help people understand what is expected. They do not require the leader to determine why an employee became quiet. Focusing on a practice within actual authority creates a practical next step without turning a sympathetic interpretation into a personal health claim or asking the team to judge a private history.

tabs.label: Qualified support
tabs.body: A person may want help that belongs with an actual assistance service or qualified clinician, rather than a meeting-design conversation. Offer the appropriate route and its real terms without promising a particular result or asking for treatment details. The service’s professional scope is different from a supervisor’s task responsibility. Both may be relevant: obtaining personal support does not automatically clarify the agenda, and a clearer agenda does not establish that no further support is wanted.

tabs.label: Formal agency process
tabs.body: A supportive conversation can reveal an accommodation request, protected-class concern, safety issue or personnel matter. That issue keeps its actual process and responsibilities; it does not become optional because the leader is using a caring tone. Explain the appropriate next route and information handling. This distinction prevents a general reflection exercise or routine check-in from delaying a specialized response, while still allowing the leader to improve unnecessary pressure in the interaction.

check.question: An employee becomes quiet in a meeting. What can the leader responsibly do?
check.correct: Examine the meeting design and offer an appropriate task-focused conversation without assuming a trauma history or diagnosis.
wrong: Announce the employee’s assumed trauma to the team.
Require a personal story before making the agenda clearer.
Ignore every work expectation because discomfort is possible.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This focuses on an observable process and leaves the person’s private history and specialized decisions outside the leader’s unsupported assumptions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Quietness does not establish a trauma history, and announcing that assumption exposes a private claim that is neither needed nor supported. Requiring a story before making the agenda clearer adds an unnecessary disclosure condition to a process choice the leader can examine directly. Ignoring every work expectation confuses respectful practice with removing actual responsibility. Review the meeting design and offer an appropriate task-focused conversation, while clinical and formal questions retain their proper routes.

items.text: Provide the meeting purpose and relevant information in advance.
Use the authorized accommodation process for a request.
Quietness proves the employee has a trauma condition.
Explain what remains open for input.
Refer a clinical question to qualified support.
A colleague’s identity reveals their personal history.

lessons.next: Next, make a required interaction more predictable and transparent.

scenario.context: A practice leader wants to make meetings more supportive, but proposes asking every employee to explain their most difficult life experience.
options: Require the stories so the leader knows who needs help.
Review the meeting’s purpose, information, participation choices and follow-through without requiring personal disclosure.
Cancel all discussions of work expectations.
responses: Personal disclosure is not necessary to improve meeting design and can add pressure. The leader is not conducting a clinical assessment.
This applies the lens to practical choices the leader controls. It supports the work while protecting personal histories.
Avoiding every expectation is not the goal. Necessary work can be discussed through a clear and respectful process.

lessons.transfer: Choose a practice leadership interaction and identify one process improvement without making a claim about a person’s history.

move.control: You can examine the interaction you control.
move.failure: The lens becomes a diagnosis or a request for private stories.
move.next: Make the practice clearer and more respectful while preserving proper routes and duties.

lessons.title: Make expectations and decisions predictable
lessons.summary: Explain purpose, scope, next steps and limits. Predictability does not require promising an outcome or withholding difficult information.
lessons.objective: Prepare a clear purpose and scope for a practice work conversation.
objectives: Prepare a clear purpose and scope for a practice work conversation.
Distinguish honest transparency from an unsupported guarantee.
Explain how a decision and next step can be communicated respectfully.
takeaways: State the purpose before asking people to participate.
Explain what is decided and what can still change.
Give an honest next step instead of a promise you cannot keep.
lessons.statement: Clarity reduces avoidable uncertainty without pretending that every outcome is settled.

image.caption: People can engage more effectively when they understand the conversation they are entering.

intro.heading: Provide the information needed to participate
intro.body:
In this example, a team receives a calendar invitation titled “Important.” No purpose or material is included. At the meeting, staff learn that a new assignment process is already selected, although the invitation seemed to imply they would help design it. The problem is not simply an anxious reaction. The leader has left the purpose, decision status and participation scope unclear.

A more transparent invitation explains the task: review a proposed handoff, identify an implementation concern or receive information about an authorized decision. Provide the relevant material through a usable channel. Do not include confidential personnel or recipient details in a general invitation. If a formal process controls notice or information, follow that process rather than inventing an informal substitute.

Be precise about the scope. “The required service standard is unchanged; we are discussing how to prepare the instruction” differs from “Everything is open.” If a decision has already been made, explain its status and the relevant reason. If input can influence an option, explain the actual question and how the input will be considered. Do not offer a choice that the process will not honor.

Transparency also includes limits. A leader may be unable to share protected information or may not yet have an answer from another role. Explain what can be said, what is pending and when an update can be expected. A return date is not a guarantee that a final decision will be available by then. If circumstances change, communicate the revised situation rather than silently allowing an old promise to stand.

Keep the tone respectful when information is difficult. Explain the work expectation, relevant basis and next route without humiliation or vague threat. Invite clarification on the task within the actual scope. A trauma-informed lens cannot guarantee that every person feels safe or agrees with the result; it can help the leader avoid unnecessary uncertainty and pressure in the process. Review whether the information was clear and usable, not whether everyone displayed the expected emotion.

inThisLesson: Explain decision status and input scope.
Communicate limits and the next update.
lessons.keyStatement: Explain what people are being asked to do, what is open and what comes next.

flashcards.back: The reason for the interaction and the task it should address. A vague invitation leaves participants to guess.
The question that participants can actually influence. Do not describe a settled decision as an open choice.
A boundary on authority, available information or disclosure. It should be explained without inventing certainty or exposing protected details.
The point at which progress or a limit will be explained. It can be useful even when a final answer is not yet available.

items.title: Write an invitation people can use
items.body: Name the task and whether the meeting informs, consults or decides. Provide necessary material with appropriate access. An accurate invitation helps participants prepare a question rather than spend the first part of the meeting guessing why they were called.

items.title: Explain a constrained choice
items.body: Sometimes a requirement is fixed but implementation details remain open. Say so. Staff can still identify a confusing handoff or missing preparation when they understand the limit. Calling the whole decision open creates a promise the leader may be unable to keep.

items.title: Respond when an answer is pending
items.body: “The responsible role has not decided; I will provide a status update” is more accurate than a reassuring invented answer. Explain any available interim instruction through the actual authority. Keep uncertainty visible without leaving staff without a work path.

tabs.heading: Match the statement to the status

tabs.label: Decided
tabs.body: The handoff direction has been authorized, while staff need to understand how it affects their next task. Explain the actual decision, relevant reason and available route for questions. Do not ask for a vote that cannot change that decision through this activity. Staff may still identify a missing instruction or implementation concern. Calling the direction decided should clarify the scope, rather than imply that every related question has been answered or that people must display agreement.

tabs.label: Open
tabs.body: The team can influence how the new instruction explains exceptions. State that question, provide suitable material and explain how input will be considered by the responsible roles. A suggestion may inform a revision or a reason for keeping wording unchanged; participation does not promise adoption or transfer approval authority. An honest open question gives people something relevant to examine. Inviting a broad redesign when only a heading can change creates a different, misleading expectation.

tabs.label: Pending
tabs.body: Another role has not yet decided whether the proposed support arrangement is feasible. Explain that dependency and what the leader can do now through actual authority, including the next status update. An update can report progress or a continued limit without promising a final decision. This makes uncertainty understandable while retaining a work path. Calling the proposal complete would leave staff planning around a resource that may not exist; pretending certainty cannot make the missing decision occur.

check.question: Which statement is most transparent?
check.correct: The service requirement is unchanged; this discussion can influence the handoff instruction, and we will explain how concerns are considered.
wrong: Everything is open, although the decision has already been made.
Nobody may ask a question because the leader is confident.
The final answer is guaranteed tomorrow despite a pending decision elsewhere.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The statement identifies the fixed requirement and the real input opportunity without overstating authority or promising the outcome.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Saying everything is open when the decision is settled offers a false choice; explain the real input scope instead. A leader’s confidence is not a reason to prohibit task questions or ignore a concern the process needs to hear. Guaranteeing tomorrow’s final answer when another role has not decided invents certainty beyond the leader’s control. State the actual requirement, the question participants can influence and an honest next update without promising adoption or a final outcome.

items.text: The meeting will identify unclear steps in a proposed instruction.
Protected personnel details will not be shared in the general update.
Vote on a decision that the process will not permit you to change.
The responsible role has approved the new handoff.
An update will explain the pending decision’s status.
Every concern will be resolved before tomorrow regardless of dependencies.

lessons.next: Next, offer meaningful participation choices without forcing disclosure.

scenario.context: A practice leader tells staff they can redesign a process, then rejects every substantive suggestion because only the title was open for comment.
options: Explain the actual scope and decision status, acknowledge the misleading invitation and provide a real route for relevant concerns.
Keep calling the discussion shared decision-making.
Demand that staff be grateful for being invited.
responses: This repairs the false expectation and gives the input an honest purpose. It does not transfer authority or promise every suggestion will be adopted.
The label exaggerates the influence available and can make future invitations less credible.
Gratitude does not resolve an inaccurate scope. Address the process and the concern respectfully.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a practice meeting invitation stating purpose, decision status, available input, relevant material and next update.

move.control: You can make the scope and next step clear.
move.failure: Participants face a vague invitation or a false choice.
move.next: Communicate the actual purpose, limits and follow-through.

lessons.title: Offer meaningful voice and choice without forced disclosure
lessons.summary: Design participation around relevant work input and genuine options. Do not make a personal story the price of being heard.
lessons.objective: Identify a genuine participation choice within a practice work process.
objectives: Identify a genuine participation choice within a practice work process.
Replace a forced personal-disclosure exercise with a task-focused activity.
Distinguish a participation option from a formal accommodation or decision requirement.
takeaways: A choice must be real and fit the work.
Relevant input does not require a personal trauma account.
Participation options do not replace formal rights and processes.
lessons.statement: Give people a usable way to contribute without requiring them to explain their private lives.

image.caption: Voice can concern a task, barrier or perspective without becoming a public personal story.

intro.heading: Make contribution possible within the actual scope
intro.body:
A practice learning session asks each employee to describe a traumatic event before discussing service practices. The facilitator says sharing proves commitment to the team. The activity is unnecessary for the work and creates pressure to disclose. A better design uses a practice case, a process question or an appropriately protected observation so staff can contribute relevant thinking without exposing a personal history.

Meaningful voice begins with an honest question. What instruction is unclear? Which perspective is missing from the proposed handoff? What tradeoff should the responsible decision consider? Ask for input that fits the task and explain its scope. Do not imply that speaking will automatically change the decision or that silence means agreement.

Offer genuine options where the work permits them. A person might contribute during the discussion or through an appropriate written route. Materials can support preparation before a meeting. A practice scenario can replace a demand for a personal example. These are suggested design choices, not permission to ignore a required participation or notice process. Confirm what is feasible and authorized in the actual setting.

Accessibility and accommodation are distinct obligations, not optional favors offered only when someone shares a story. Use the actual accommodation route when relevant. Under MMB’s accommodation policy, initial requests do not require a particular form or special vocabulary. Subsequent appropriate process documentation and decision requirements still apply; medical documentation has designated responsibilities. A supervisor should not turn a general participation exercise into a medical-information request.

Respect cultural and individual variation without assuming preferences from identity. Some people may want time to reflect; others may prefer a live conversation. Ask about relevant process needs rather than assigning one style to a group. Native American- and Tribal-specific subject matter is referred to the appropriate office within ADSA under the owner’s direction; this general leadership course does not teach that specialized process.

Retain accountability for the work. If a task genuinely requires a response, state that expectation and provide an appropriate route. A meaningful choice concerns the available method or input within real limits; it is not a promise that every responsibility can be declined. The goal is to avoid unnecessary coercion while making the work more understandable and usable.

inThisLesson: Preserve access and formal process duties.
lessons.keyStatement: Meaningful voice is relevant input through a real route, not compulsory personal disclosure.

flashcards.back: An option that the process can actually honor. Explain its limits rather than offering a choice only in name.
Information or reasoning about the work. It can be valuable without a personal account of trauma or identity.
Pressure to share private experience as a condition of participation or credibility. Avoid it in a general learning or work activity.
The authorized process for a disability-related request. General participation design does not replace its requirements or justify supervisor medical-information collection.

items.title: Use a practice case
items.body: A case about a confusing service instruction can teach the same analytical skill without asking an employee to disclose a personal experience. Invite different interpretations of the task and explain that the scenario is practice, not an allegation about a colleague.

items.title: Provide a usable input route
items.body: If the actual process permits written input, give a clear question and the appropriate destination. Do not create a separate unprotected channel for confidential information. A choice is useful only when someone can understand and use it within the stated scope.

items.title: Separate silence from agreement
items.body: A participant may be reflecting, unsure of the scope or choosing not to share. Silence does not establish consent or satisfaction. When a response is required, state the task expectation directly rather than inferring a person’s position from participation style.

tabs.label: General design choice
tabs.body: Replacing a demand for personal trauma stories with a practice handoff case preserves the analytical skill while removing an unnecessary disclosure condition. Relevant advance information or a feasible written input route may also help people prepare. These are choices within the activity’s actual scope, not guarantees of every participant’s experience. Explain which methods can genuinely be offered and where input goes, so an appealing participation option is usable rather than merely named.

tabs.label: Formal requirement
tabs.body: Some work requires a response or an applicable notice and decision process. State that requirement and the available method honestly rather than suggesting that every responsibility can be declined. For example, the team may choose how to discuss an instruction while the underlying required step remains. A real choice operates within those limits. The course does not invent a new required activity or remove an existing one; the appropriate actual process establishes what applies.

tabs.label: Protected request
tabs.body: An initial accommodation request can be made in ordinary language without a particular form. That opens the actual process; it does not mean subsequent appropriate documentation and decision steps disappear. Promptly forward the request and identify the appropriate decision maker under the actual procedure. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation; any appropriate request belongs with the agency ADA Coordinator. A group exercise or personal story is neither proof required to recognize the request nor a substitute for its proper handling.

check.question: Which activity best supports meaningful voice without unnecessary disclosure?
check.correct: Use a practice work case with clear questions and feasible input routes, while keeping formal access and task requirements in place.
wrong: Require every employee to tell a trauma story to demonstrate commitment.
Assume silence means full consent to the final decision.
Assign participation preferences to employees based only on identity.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The activity gives people a relevant way to reason about the work without asking for private histories or overstating the meaning of participation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A compulsory trauma story adds disclosure pressure without being necessary to practice the work skill. Silence does not establish consent; a person may be reflecting, unsure or choosing not to share, while any actual required response should be stated directly. Presumed identity also cannot establish an individual’s preferred method. Use a practice work case, clear questions and feasible genuine routes, with the actual access and task requirements retained.

items.text: Use a practice handoff case instead of personal trauma stories.
Forward an accommodation request through the actual process.
Public disclosure proves a person is committed.
Explain a feasible written input option and its scope.
State the actual required response accurately.
A person’s identity tells us which method they prefer.

lessons.next: Next, handle a difficult conversation with clarity and accountability.

scenario.context: In this example, a facilitator asks staff to reveal painful personal experiences. An employee requests a practice case instead, and the facilitator calls the request resistance.
options: Insist on the disclosure so the learning feels authentic.
Adopt a relevant practice case and explain how staff can practice the skill without private disclosure.
Assume the employee needs a clinical diagnosis.
responses: The skill can be taught through the work question without compulsory disclosure. Authenticity does not require exposing private histories.
This preserves the learning purpose while removing an unnecessary demand. The facilitator should not assign motive to the request.
The request concerns activity design. It does not establish a health condition or authorize assessment.

lessons.transfer: Redesign a practice disclosure-based activity with a work case, clear question, genuine input option and applicable formal route.

move.control: You can make participation relevant and less intrusive.
move.failure: Voice becomes a demand to expose private experience.
move.next: Use real task choices and preserve access, privacy and actual responsibilities.

lessons.title: Handle difficult conversations with care and accountability
lessons.summary: State the work concern clearly, allow relevant response and avoid humiliation. Respectful practice does not remove actual standards or reporting duties.
lessons.objective: Prepare a factual, respectful opening for a practice difficult conversation.
objectives: Prepare a factual, respectful opening for a practice difficult conversation.
Separate a work expectation from assumptions about character or health.
Identify a matter that requires a formal route rather than an informal repair alone.
takeaways: Use relevant facts and a clear purpose.
Allow response without demanding agreement or a private history.
An informal conversation cannot replace a required formal process.
lessons.statement: A difficult message can be direct without being humiliating or speculative.

image.caption: Care and accountability can be part of the same work conversation.

intro.heading: Keep the conversation about the actual concern
intro.body:
In this example, a supervisor needs to address repeated incomplete handoffs. The supervisor prepares a public announcement that the employee is unreliable and emotionally incapable of the work. The announcement contains unsupported judgments and exposes an individual concern to the wrong audience. A more responsible response follows the actual personnel process and focuses on the relevant task evidence, expectation and opportunity to respond.

A trauma-informed lens does not decide the merits of the personnel issue. It can help a leader examine how the interaction is conducted: appropriate setting, clear purpose, relevant information, respectful language and honest next steps. Those practices do not replace notice, representation, documentation or other requirements that may apply. Consult the authorized roles rather than creating a course-based disciplinary procedure.

State what is known about the work. Identify the expectation and the specific concern using appropriately handled information. Do not infer a disability, trauma history, cultural motive or character trait from the event. Give the employee the relevant opportunity to respond through the actual process. Listening to that information does not mean the leader must agree with every interpretation; it means the decision should not rest on an avoidable assumption.

Avoid making emotional performance part of the standard. A person does not have to display gratitude, calmness or a preferred participation style to make their task information relevant. At the same time, supportive practice does not excuse prohibited conduct or remove legitimate expectations. Handle any actual misconduct or protected matter through its proper route. MMB’s Respectful Workplace Policy 1432 concerns matters within its scope. Protected-class harassment and discrimination have the separate Policy 1436 path: supervisors and managers immediately report all allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and comply with agency complaint and investigation procedures. Assigned authorized investigation duties remain intact. Do not replace these responsibilities with a generic mediation exercise.

If the conversation reveals a possible accommodation, safety or required reporting issue, use the actual process promptly. A private conversation or apology cannot automatically settle it. Keep the appropriate information protected and explain the next step. The goal is a clear, accountable interaction that avoids unnecessary humiliation and unsupported claims, not a guarantee that no difficult feelings will arise.

inThisLesson: Use an appropriate setting and process.
lessons.keyStatement: Respectful accountability addresses the work through the actual process without diagnosing or humiliating the person.

flashcards.back: Information that bears on the task concern and is handled appropriately. Distinguish it from a conclusion about character or personal history.
Clear expectations and authorized follow-through. It can be respectful without becoming optional or punitive by assumption.
The appropriate chance to provide relevant information through the actual process. It does not require agreement with the leader’s interpretation.
The procedure suited to the concern, including personnel, accommodation, safety or reporting requirements. Informal repair is not always enough.

items.title: Check the audience and setting
items.body: An individual work concern usually should not become a public team lesson. Follow the actual process for who participates and what information is shared. A desire for transparency does not authorize disclosure of protected personnel details.

items.title: Remove assumptions from the opening
items.body: Replace “You do not care” with the relevant handoff fact and expectation. The employee’s response may reveal missing information or an explanation the leader had not considered. It may also confirm a concern that needs formal follow-through; listen without predetermining either result.

items.title: Do not force a repair activity
items.body: A group apology, mediated conversation or reflective exercise may be inappropriate when a formal issue requires action. Consult the responsible route. A supportive tone should not be used to pressure someone to abandon a complaint or protected request.

tabs.label: Clarification
tabs.body: The employee may have received conflicting handoff instructions. Clarify the relevant expectation through the responsible role and consider the information that bears on the task. An unclear instruction is not evidence that the employee is emotionally incapable or does not care. The clarification may resolve the confusion or show that another work question remains. Keeping the task and interpretation separate helps the leader choose a proportionate response without prematurely deciding a personnel outcome.

tabs.label: Personnel action
tabs.body: A documented concern may require an authorized personnel process, with whatever notice, response, representation or documentation requirements actually apply. A respectful setting and factual opening can improve the interaction but do not establish a new disciplinary procedure. Consult the responsible roles and preserve assigned duties, including authorized investigation where applicable. This distinguishes care in how the conversation occurs from the separate evidence and authority needed for an employment decision.

tabs.label: Protected or safety concern
tabs.body: A protected-class allegation keeps its separate reporting and complaint route. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors immediately report all such allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency procedures. An apology, cultural discussion or reconciliation exercise cannot postpone that duty. Accommodation and safety issues have their own appropriate processes as well. A caring interaction can accompany formal action without pressuring the person to withdraw the concern or assuming an informal repair settles it.

check.question: Which opening best supports respectful accountability?
check.correct: I want to discuss this documented handoff concern and the applicable expectation through the proper process, and hear the relevant information you can provide.
wrong: You are emotionally incapable, and the team needs to know.
You must agree with my interpretation before you can respond.
A group apology will replace any formal reporting requirement.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This focuses on the actual work and proper process while allowing relevant information. It avoids character or clinical judgments.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Calling an employee emotionally incapable assigns an unsupported personal explanation and publicly exposes an individual concern. Requiring agreement before a response blocks potentially relevant information; hearing the person does not require accepting every interpretation. A group apology cannot replace an applicable formal process: managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under MMB Policy 1436. Keep the discussion factual, protect information and follow actual assigned procedures.

items.text: State the relevant expectation and documented task concern.
Use the actual accommodation process when a request arises.
Publicly label the employee as traumatized.
Hear relevant information before deciding through the proper process.
A required reporting matter cannot be closed by an informal apology alone.
Require gratitude as proof the employee accepted feedback.

lessons.next: Next, offer appropriate support and explain its boundaries.

scenario.context: In this example, an employee raises a possible protected-class harassment concern during a work conversation. The leader proposes an informal team exercise and asks the employee to drop the issue.
options: Use the appropriate formal route and protect relevant information; a supportive interaction must not pressure the employee to abandon the concern.
Require a reconciliation activity instead of the applicable process.
Explain that trauma-informed leadership means formal concerns are unnecessary.
responses: This retains the concern and actual responsibilities. The supervisor or manager immediately reports the protected-class allegation or incident to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under MMB Policy 1436 and follows agency procedures. A supportive conversation can accompany that action but cannot pressure the employee to abandon the concern or delay the report.
An informal activity cannot be assumed to replace required handling and can add pressure to the original concern.
The lens informs how people are treated; it does not erase policy or reporting obligations.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice difficult-conversation opening with relevant facts, a clear expectation, an appropriate response opportunity and a formal-route check.

move.control: You can make accountability factual and respectful.
move.failure: A difficult concern becomes public humiliation or an assumed diagnosis.
move.next: Use the proper process and listen without replacing formal duties with an informal activity.

lessons.title: Offer support and preserve role boundaries
lessons.summary: Help people find an appropriate route without becoming a clinician, collecting a private history or promising absolute confidentiality.
lessons.objective: Match a practice work or support question to an appropriate route.
objectives: Match a practice work or support question to an appropriate route.
Explain why a leader should not collect a trauma history or treatment record in a learning exercise.
Prepare an honest support offer and next work action.
takeaways: Offer the actual support route without pressure.
Clinical help, accommodation and work planning are distinct.
Explain information-handling limits rather than promising absolute secrecy.
lessons.statement: Support is most useful when the person understands the route, purpose and limits.

image.caption: A referral can accompany a practical work response without turning the leader into a clinician.

intro.heading: Know what help you can offer
intro.body:
A practice leader wants to help an employee after a difficult service situation. The leader offers to assess the employee’s trauma and asks for treatment records in the project folder. This crosses roles and places sensitive information in an inappropriate location. The leader can instead acknowledge the work concern, explain available appropriate support and address the task through the proper process.

MMB’s Leadership and Team Dynamics page provides a current state resource for leaders and points employees toward assistance. Use the actual page for access and review its service terms. Do not invent a provider, promise a specific clinical outcome or tell staff that confidentiality has no exceptions. A leader should also avoid demanding proof that an employee used a voluntary resource as a sign of cooperation. Any actual direction or required action needs its authorized basis and process.

Keep work planning visible. If a difficult situation exposes an unclear instruction or an unresolved handoff, the team can examine that issue with appropriately protected information. Offering assistance does not settle the process question. Likewise, an improved instruction does not mean an employee no longer needs any personal support. The two responses can coexist without requiring the leader to determine a diagnosis.

Accommodation is another distinct route. Follow MMB’s actual policy and designated responsibilities when a request arises. Do not ask the employee to disclose trauma publicly or provide medical documentation to a supervisor in a general learning discussion. Explain the proper contact through the agency’s actual process and forward the request as required.

State what information is appropriate for each purpose. A learning worksheet uses practice facts. A general work-improvement record contains task details needed for the improvement, not private clinical information. A formal case follows its required handling. If an actual urgent safety concern occurs, use the immediate appropriate response rather than waiting for ordinary support scheduling. A thoughtful offer makes the next route understandable while preserving the employee’s privacy, actual rights and the leader’s role limits.

inThisLesson: Use the current appropriate support resource.
Keep work and personal support distinct.
lessons.keyStatement: Offer help within its actual scope, and keep the work concern and private information in their proper processes.

flashcards.back: A clear explanation of an appropriate resource and its actual route. It should not require proof of private treatment in a learning activity.
The limit on what a leader, clinician or designated formal role does. Good intentions do not remove that limit.
The reason information is needed and where it belongs. Clinical details do not belong in an ordinary project or practice record.
Personal support and an authorized work improvement can occur together. Neither automatically resolves the other question.

accordion.heading: Make the offer clear and respectful

items.title: Use the actual resource
items.body: Link to the current official assistance page or use the agency’s known authorized route. Explain what kind of help the page offers without promising a clinical result. Access details can change, so an invented name or number is not a useful shortcut.

items.title: Do not request proof of voluntary help
items.body: An employee’s choice to use assistance is not a learning score or a loyalty test. Continue to address legitimate work expectations through the proper process. If a formal action has requirements, consult the authorized role rather than imposing an informal proof demand.

items.title: Keep the work action separate
items.body: A person may accept support while the team clarifies a service instruction. Record the instruction question, owner and next update in an appropriate work note. Do not add the employee’s private support use or history to make the note seem complete.

tabs.heading: Choose the route by the purpose

tabs.label: Task support
tabs.body: The difficult service situation may reveal an unclear instruction or missing handoff responsibility. Examine that task with the relevant work role and appropriately protected information. Name who will clarify it and what happens next. This is useful even if the employee does not discuss personal history or use assistance. The work response cannot assess trauma, and an offer of counseling cannot establish which instruction the team should follow; each question needs its appropriate purpose.

tabs.label: Personal assistance
tabs.body: Offer the actual current assistance resource and point to its access and confidentiality terms. Do not make voluntary use a learning score, loyalty test or condition for hearing a work concern. The person can decide whether that resource is useful without reporting treatment details to the project. A separate formal direction, if actually applicable, retains its authorized basis and procedure. Keeping those distinctions clear makes the offer understandable without misrepresenting its purpose or collecting unnecessary private information.

tabs.label: Formal request or concern
tabs.body: A request or concern may need accommodation handling, personnel review, safety response or required reporting. Recognize that purpose and connect it to the appropriate actual process rather than calling the assistance offer sufficient. Explain role and information limits, and do not place private case information in a learning worksheet. A formal response and a practical work clarification may continue in parallel. The supportive tone matters, but it cannot approve a request, waive duties or promise absolute secrecy.

check.question: Which support offer is most appropriate?
check.correct: Here is the current official assistance route; we can also clarify the work question through the proper process, without putting private health details in the project record.
wrong: Give me your treatment records so I can assess your trauma.
Using voluntary assistance will determine your course score.
I promise no information will ever need a formal safety or reporting route.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The offer distinguishes support and work planning, protects private information and avoids a blanket promise about matters outside the leader’s control.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Requesting treatment records to assess trauma crosses the leader’s role and places sensitive material outside a legitimate task purpose. Making voluntary assistance determine a course score turns support into pressure rather than an understandable resource offer. Promising that information can never need a safety or reporting route may conflict with actual duties. Offer the current resource and its real terms, address the separate work concern and preserve appropriate formal handling without unnecessary personal disclosure.

sorting.heading: Match information to its proper use

items.text: A practice case describes an unclear service instruction.
A clinical question is directed to qualified help.
Treatment records are copied into the team project folder.
A work note names the responsible role for clarifying the handoff.
An accommodation request follows the designated process.
Staff must reveal trauma histories to earn a learning score.

lessons.next: Next, review leadership practices without declaring a checklist proves transformation.

scenario.context: A practice leader offers assistance but refuses to examine an instruction problem unless the employee reports whether they attended counseling.
options: Require the counseling report as a condition of work clarification.
Drop all work expectations because help was offered.
Keep voluntary support separate and examine the task concern through the appropriate work process without requesting private treatment information.
responses: The work concern can be examined without treatment details. An informal condition adds pressure and crosses purpose boundaries.
Appropriate support does not erase legitimate responsibilities. Address them through the actual process.
This allows both questions to be addressed within their proper roles. The leader should not turn support use into evidence for a learning or loyalty judgment.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a practice support offer with the actual type of route, a privacy boundary and a separate next action on the work concern.

move.control: You can offer help and a clear work response.
move.failure: Support becomes clinical overreach or a disclosure condition.
move.next: Use the appropriate route and keep information matched to its legitimate purpose.

lessons.title: Review the practice and make a concrete improvement
lessons.summary: Examine whether a leadership process became clearer and more usable. Do not infer trauma outcomes or universal safety from attendance or silence.
lessons.objective: Choose a process question for a practice leadership improvement.
objectives: Choose a process question for a practice leadership improvement.
Identify an unsupported conclusion about safety, health or consent.
Prepare an appropriately protected improvement note with evidence limits and a next step.
takeaways: A completed activity does not establish a whole organizational approach.
Silence or attendance cannot prove safety or agreement.
Review the practical process and explain what remains unknown.
lessons.statement: Review what changed in the interaction, not what you assume changed inside a person.

image.caption: A thoughtful improvement note makes a practical action and its limits visible.

intro.heading: Keep improvement claims proportionate
intro.body:
In this example, a team completes a leadership workshop. The project report says the organization is now trauma-informed and every employee feels safe. The evidence is insufficient. Attendance shows participation in an activity, not a complete organizational approach or every person’s experience. CDC’s summary cautions that continuing organizational attention matters; a checklist alone is not enough.

Choose a specific leadership practice to review. If the action was clearer meeting scope, examine whether invitations identify purpose and whether the discussion stays within that scope. If the action replaced forced personal stories with practice cases, check whether the activity actually uses practice information and offers a relevant task question. These observations can inform a practical improvement without becoming a clinical measure.

Seek appropriate feedback on the process. Was the material usable? Was the next step clear? Did the input route work? Do not ask for private trauma histories to prove the design mattered. Do not treat a lack of response as satisfaction, consent or absence of concern. Explain the evidence limit and consider a feasible, appropriately protected next feedback route.

Look for a new problem created by the change. A participation option may be unclear about whether a response is required. A more detailed invitation may accidentally include protected information. A private conversation may still omit the actual formal route. Review the whole process rather than judging only the appealing part of the design.

Use a concise improvement note: intended practice, actual action, appropriate observation, unresolved issue and next responsible step. Keep personal employee, recipient and clinical information out of general learning records. A before-and-after difference does not establish cause by itself, and a positive account does not represent everyone.

Sustaining the lens means continuing to examine leadership choices and actual responsibilities. It does not require a public label or a demand that staff report the expected emotions. Choose one concrete revision, explain the reason and check its effect through the appropriate process. The review should make practice more thoughtful and accountable without overstating what the evidence can establish.

inThisLesson: State missing information and claim limits.
lessons.keyStatement: Report the practical action and its evidence honestly; do not convert it into an unsupported health or organizational claim.

flashcards.back: Evidence about an interaction, such as a clear agenda or usable input route. It is not automatically evidence of a personal health outcome.
A count showing an activity occurred. It does not establish organizational transformation, safety or agreement.
Something the review cannot establish, including missing feedback or uncertain cause. State it rather than filling the gap with a reassuring conclusion.
A concrete authorized revision to the practice with a responsible role and review question. It should not require private trauma disclosure.

items.title: Choose a concrete question
items.body: “Do invitations accurately explain the discussion scope?” can be examined in the actual process. “Is everyone healed?” is neither the purpose nor something this course equips the leader to determine. A task question supports useful action without a clinical claim.

items.title: Protect feedback
items.body: Collect only information appropriate to the purpose and use the authorized handling. A small group or recognizable story can identify someone even without a name. Do not publish private experiences in a progress narrative merely to make the result more engaging.

items.title: Explain an unresolved concern
items.body: A review may find that staff still do not know how their input will be considered. Name that issue and the next process action. Do not hide it under a positive participation figure or interpret uncertainty as personal resistance.

tabs.label: Action completed
tabs.body: The workshop occurred, the activity now uses practice cases or the invitation includes an accurate purpose. Those observations support a delivery or implementation statement. They do not reveal every participant’s understanding or feelings. Confirming the action is still useful: it distinguishes what actually changed from a proposal. Then ask a relevant process question, such as whether the discussion stayed within the stated scope, rather than treating completion as evidence of organizational certification.

tabs.label: Process evidence
tabs.body: Appropriate observations may show that invitations identify the real input question, while feedback may reveal people still cannot tell where written comments go. Retain both findings and their scope. Check the task, context, information handling and who was heard before extending the conclusion. The evidence can support a targeted clarification without diagnosing anyone or proving cause. Missing feedback remains unknown; a positive participation figure does not settle the experience of people who did not respond.

tabs.label: Unsupported conclusion
tabs.body: A high attendance count cannot establish that a workshop healed trauma or that every person feels safe. Receiving no feedback likewise cannot establish consent or the absence of concerns. These are different unsupported inferences, not simply alternative labels for the same finding. Report the actual action and appropriately examined process instead. That leaves room to improve the practice and use proper formal routes without turning employees’ private experiences into proof for a broad organizational claim.

check.question: A workshop is complete and several staff have not provided feedback. What can the report accurately say?
check.correct: The activity occurred; describe the specific process changes and evidence limits without inferring every person’s safety, consent or health outcome.
wrong: Everyone feels safe because the attendance count is high.
The organization is certified trauma-informed by this checklist.
People who did not reply have no concerns.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This reports the action and limits proportionately, leaving personal outcomes and broader organizational conclusions unclaimed.
check.feedbackIncorrect: High attendance establishes participation in an activity, not every person’s feeling of safety. A checklist does not certify an organization-wide trauma-informed approach; the source describes continuing organizational attention. Receiving no reply from some participants leaves their experience unknown, rather than showing that they have no concerns. Report the actual practice, useful scoped observations and missing evidence, then choose a proportionate next process question without requesting private histories.

items.text: The revised invitation states the actual input scope.
No feedback was received from some participants, so their experience is unknown.
A workshop cured every employee’s trauma.
The practice activity uses practice cases rather than personal histories.
The team will clarify how written input is considered.
A checklist proves the whole agency is trauma-informed.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to choose one respectful leadership practice and review it carefully.

scenario.context: A practice project report uses a high attendance count to declare universal psychological safety and publishes a recognizable employee story as evidence.
options: Keep the claim because the story is compelling.
Report the actual practice and evidence limits, remove inappropriate identifying detail and choose a proportionate next review question.
Require every employee to provide a more personal story.
responses: A compelling account does not establish every person’s experience and may expose private information. Revise both the claim and the handling.
This makes the report accurate and appropriately protected. A concrete practice question is more useful than an unsupported universal conclusion.
More intrusive disclosure does not repair the inference. Keep the evidence matched to the legitimate process purpose.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice improvement note with the leadership practice, action, appropriate observation, evidence limit and next step. Include no private history.

move.control: You can make improvement visible and accurate.
move.failure: Attendance or silence becomes a health, safety or certification claim.
move.next: Review the specific practice and protect information while naming the next useful action.

jobAid.subtitle: A thoughtful leadership interaction
remember: Examine the practice without assuming a personal history or diagnosis.
Make purpose, scope, choices and next steps clear.
Keep accountability and formal duties in place.
Offer support through its actual route without forced disclosure.

sections.heading: Before the interaction
items: What is the actual work purpose and applicable process?
What information and preparation are relevant and usable?
What is decided, open or pending?
What genuine participation choices are available?

sections.heading: During the interaction
items: State facts and expectations without humiliating or diagnosing.
Ask about the task, not a private trauma history.
Listen to relevant information without treating silence as consent.

Use the proper formal route for protected, personnel or safety concerns. Managers and supervisors immediately report Policy 1436 allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency procedures.

sections.heading: After the interaction
items: Explain the next work action and authority limit.
Offer the current appropriate support resource where useful.
Keep private information out of general learning records.
Review the practical process and evidence limits rather than claiming universal safety or health outcomes.
